title: Independence, Interdependence, and Worldview
intro: The holistic lens behind First Nations political life. Questions 16-18 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: Focused on the whole of creation rather than individual parts. In First Nations worldviews, people are one part of the universe, no more or less important than any other.
A people's basic understanding of how the world works and how humans should live in it.
Mutual reliance within and between groups. No person or nation survives alone, so independence is always balanced with responsibility to others.

body: In general, First Nations worldviews are holistic. The Creator put humans on Earth with everything needed for a good life, and in return humans must respect natural laws learned over generations by close observation. People are simply one part of the universe, no more or less important than any other.

That lens explains the politics. Early treaties reflect mutual respect, independence, and interdependence between sovereign groups and the land. Groups must be interdependent because no one survives alone, which is why interacting with another group in another territory meant negotiating relationship, not asserting ownership.

The Creator's laws arrive the same way: learned over generations by close observation of how the world works, then carried in story and ceremony. Respecting natural laws is not separate from government; for peoples whose leaders, laws, hunts, and ceremonies form one fabric, the worldview is the constitution.

Person and people differ the same way part and whole differ. A person is an individual; a people shares identity, history, territory, and continuity across generations. Rights attach to the people because the history that created them belongs to no single lifetime.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 16-18 ask what holistic means, why groups must be interdependent, and how First Nations viewed other territories. Answer all three from the two paragraphs above.

check.prompt: How does a holistic worldview shape relations between groups?
check.sample: Sample response: because every part of creation matters and no group survives alone, relations are negotiated as mutual respect and interdependence rather than domination.

title: Early Treaties and Relationships Among Nations
intro: Treaties between First Nations before European domination. Complete Assignment 1.1 after this lesson.

terms.def: A formal agreement between nations that sets out how each will relate to the other and share resources.
An alliance of nations living in peace under shared law, such as the five-nation Haudenosaunee confederacy.

body: Early treaties reflect traditional values: mutual respect, independence, and interdependence between sovereign groups. Before 1450, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca formed the Great Law of Peace confederacy after years of nation-against-nation conflict, recording it in wampum.

The pattern continued with Europeans. The 1645 Guswentah (Two Row Wampum) treaty with the Dutch modelled peaceful co-existence, and in 1844 Cuthbert Grant answered Dakota demands for compensation with an offer of peace instead. Treaties sorted out how each nation would relate to others and share resources.

Recording mattered as much as promising. Wampum belts and strings carried the terms in shell patterns a trained reader could recite, and smoking the pipe sealed many agreements the way signatures seal European contracts. When later disputes turned on what was agreed, the question was always which record counted: the belt, the ceremony, the memory, or the paper.

The Great Law itself shows scale. Five nations at war with one another accepted one law of peace before 1450, ending nation-against-nation conflict across their territories. Confederacy was not surrender of identity; each nation kept itself while sharing the law, the earliest model in this course of distinct peoples governing together.

check.prompt: What values do early treaties show, and how were they recorded?
check.sample: Sample response: mutual respect, independence, and interdependence, recorded in wampum belts and strings, sealed at times with pipe-smoking ceremonies rather than signatures.

title: Colonization, the Royal Proclamation, and Confederation
intro: How power tilted, and the two documents that still matter. Questions 24-27 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: One people's imposition of control over another's land and life. The textbook describes two types; both shifted power toward Euro-Canadian governments in the nineteenth century.
The British statement recognizing First Nations land rights and setting the Crown as intermediary. Still significant today and echoed in the 1982 Charter.

body: The textbook describes two types of colonization, and both tilted nineteenth-century power toward settlers through numbers, displacement, and imposed ways of life. European and First Nations worldviews clashed underneath: Europeans saw treaties as business contracts while First Nations saw sacred oaths, sealed with ceremonies such as pipe smoking rather than signatures.

The Royal Proclamation of 1763 belongs to the earlier co-operation stage and is still significant because it recognized First Nations land rights and is echoed in the 1982 Charter. It also set a paternalistic pattern, installing the Crown as the decider between First Nations and settlers. The British North America Act of 1867 then created the Dominion of Canada, and a century later Aboriginal leaders watched its patriation closely for threats to their rights.

Colonization came in two gears. One planted settlers who displaced peoples by numbers and occupation; the other ruled at a distance through agents, laws, and imposed administration. Both tilted power the same way, and both provoked the same response: peoples defending nationhood with the tools at hand, from council fires to courtrooms.

The BNA Act's long shadow is the reason patriation alarmed Aboriginal leaders. If the constitution is the rule-book for who decides, then bringing it home without entrenching Aboriginal and treaty rights could lock in a century of exclusion permanently. That fear drove the constitutional battles of Block C.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 26-27 ask why each document still matters. Answer with recognition-plus-paternalism for the Proclamation and constitutional-foundation-plus-patriation-watch for the BNA Act.

check.prompt: Why is the Royal Proclamation still significant today?
check.sample: Sample response: it recognized First Nations land rights, set the Crown-treaty relationship still invoked today, and is echoed in the 1982 Charter.
